prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

JAKARTA, Indonesia (CNN) -- Heavy rains smashed through a dam near Indonesia's capital Friday, unleashing a torrent of water that plowed into hundreds of homes and killed at least 52 people in what some survivors described as a suburban "tsunami." Members of a search and rescue team look for bodies around upended trees and vehicles near  Jakarta Friday. Sleeping residents were taken by surprise by the powerful flash flood as it crashed through Jakarta's crowded Cirendeu suburb, in the early hours of the morning. Rescue crews suspended their search for survivors overnight Friday evening, the National Disaster Coordination Agency said. The agency put the death toll at 52 with 17 missing. It said 33 people were injured and 1,490 left homeless. The Indonesian Health Ministry put the death toll higher at 58 people. After the deluge, drenched, injured and shivering survivors took refuge on the rooftops of their homes as rescuers in rubber boats struggled to reach them. Social affairs spokesman official Mardjito, who like many Indonesians goes by one name, said relief efforts were being hampered by debris from the dam. "We're still trying to get into the houses, but the problem is, mud is getting in our way," he said. Pictures from the scene showed the pulverized ruins of wooden buildings emerging as brown muddied waters subside.  Watch scenes of the flood devastation » . Indonesian President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono, currently on the campaign trail ahead of elections later this year, said he had ordered senior ministers to visit the scene of the disaster. "On behalf of the government, I express my condolences to the families of the dead victims and may their souls be accepted by God almighty," he said, according to the official Antara news agency. The rain obliterated a 255-meter-long section of the dam at around 4 am local time, releasing a wall of water from the 20-hectare lake that some survivors said reminded them of the tsunami that hit Indonesia in 2004. "They said they had heard loud rumbling sounds like during a powerful earthquake. They later found out that the sounds came from the water rushing out from the dam's lake," Antara said. Survivors told stories of dead relatives and harrowing brushes with death as they struggled to escape rising waters. Dewi Masitoh, a 40-year-old housewife, told the AFP news agency that she escaped with her husband and two daughters after they saw rising water reach the door of their stilt house. "We were on the second floor but my daughter went back downstairs when the window broke and water gushed in. My husband jumped in and pulled her out of the water by her neck. "I punched a hole through the roof and we all climbed up through," she said, showing cuts and scratches on her arms." Floods from heavy rains are an annual occurrence around Jakarta, a low lying city on the northern coast of Java island, where poor infrastructure often results in polluted canals and rivers spilling their banks and spilling into thousands of homes. In 2007, 38 people were killed and 430,000 forced from their homes when storm waters three meters deep in some places swamped 75 percent of the capital, which is home to about 9 million people. With poor sanitation and a hot and humid climate, the risk of water-borne diseases is usually a major concern following floods in the city, where mosquito-transmitted malaria is also a threat. CNN's Andy Saputra contributed to this report.

# Dam Collapse Triggers Deadly Flash Flood Near Jakarta, Dozens Dead

**Jakarta, Indonesia** — A catastrophic dam failure unleashed a wall of water across communities on the outskirts of Indonesia's capital, killing at least 47 people and displacing thousands, officials said Thursday, as rescue teams raced to find survivors trapped in the debris of collapsed homes.

The dam, located in a densely populated area south of Jakarta, gave way in the early morning hours following days of torrential rain that overwhelmed the aging structure. Floodwaters surged through residential neighborhoods while many residents were still asleep.

## 'The Water Came in Seconds'

Survivors described scenes of terror as the flood swept away everything in its path.

"I heard a loud crack, like thunder, and then the water came in seconds," said Siti Rahayu, 34, who escaped to her rooftop with her two children. "There was no time to save anything. I could hear my neighbors screaming in the dark."

Ahmad Fauzi, a 52-year-old shopkeeper, lost his home and business in minutes. "Everything I worked for is gone," he said, standing amid the mud where his store once stood. "We are alive, thank God, but we have nothing left."

Emergency shelters have been set up in mosques, schools, and government buildings, where an estimated 8,000 displaced residents are seeking refuge.

## Official Response

The National Disaster Mitigation Agency (BNPB) confirmed the death toll was expected to rise as search operations continued.

"Our priority right now is search and rescue and providing emergency aid to affected families," said BNPB spokesperson Abdul Muhari in a statement. "We have deployed hundreds of personnel, along with boats and heavy equipment."

Indonesian President Joko Widodo expressed condolences and ordered an immediate investigation into the dam's failure. "We must determine what happened and ensure this tragedy is not repeated," he said during a visit to the disaster zone.

Local officials acknowledged that concerns about the dam's structural integrity had been raised in previous years but said maintenance had been delayed due to budget constraints.

## A City Prone to Flooding

The disaster underscores Jakarta's long-standing vulnerability to flooding, a problem experts say has been worsened by rapid urbanization, poor infrastructure, and climate change.

Home to more than 10 million people, Jakarta is one of the fastest-sinking cities in the world. Excessive extraction of groundwater has caused parts of the city to subside by several centimeters each year, while much of northern Jakarta already sits below sea level.

Seasonal monsoon rains regularly trigger flooding, but scientists warn that increasingly intense rainfall driven by climate change is straining the region's outdated water management systems.

"Jakarta's flood problems are the result of decades of unchecked development and neglected infrastructure," said environmental researcher Dr. Nurul Hidayat. "Events like this are a warning that we can no longer afford to postpone serious investment in flood defenses and dam safety."

The chronic flooding is one of the reasons Indonesia is relocating its capital to Nusantara, a new city being built on the island of Borneo. However, critics argue the move does little to address the risks faced by the millions who remain in Jakarta.

## Recovery Efforts Ahead

As waters begin to recede, officials warn that the humanitarian crisis is far from over. Concerns are mounting over the spread of waterborne diseases, and aid organizations are appealing for clean water, food, and medical supplies.

The Indonesian Red Cross has mobilized volunteers to assist with relief efforts, while neighboring regions have pledged support.

For survivors like Siti Rahayu, the road to recovery feels uncertain. "We will start again," she said quietly. "But I don't know how."

*This is a developing story and will be updated.*

Jakarta, home to some 10 million people, is among the world's most flood-prone megacities and is sinking at an alarming rate due to excessive groundwater extraction. The government has cited such vulnerabilities as part of its rationale for relocating the national capital to a new site on Borneo.

## An Uncertain Recovery

As the water slowly receded on Tuesday, residents returned to survey the wreckage of their homes, salvaging what few belongings remained caked in mud. Many said they had received no warning before the floods struck.

"We lost everything, but we are alive," said Ahmad Fauzi, 55, standing outside his gutted home. "I only pray they find those who are still missing."

Meteorological authorities warned that further heavy rainfall was expected in the coming days, raising fears of additional flooding as the region enters the peak of its monsoon season.

# Dam Collapse Near Jakarta Unleashes Deadly Floods After Torrential Overnight Rains

**JAKARTA** — A dam on the outskirts of Indonesia's capital gave way in the pre-dawn hours Thursday after days of relentless rainfall overwhelmed the aging structure, sending a wall of water through several densely populated neighborhoods and forcing thousands to flee their homes in the darkness.

Local authorities reported that the breach occurred shortly after 4:00 a.m. local time, when many residents were still asleep. The sudden surge inundated low-lying communities within minutes, catching families off guard and complicating early rescue efforts.

## Scenes of Chaos in the Early Morning

Emergency crews, aided by soldiers and volunteers, worked through the morning to evacuate stranded residents, many of whom scrambled onto rooftops as the floodwaters rose. Rubber boats navigated streets that had transformed into murky rivers, while the sound of sirens echoed across the affected districts.

"I woke up to my neighbors screaming," said Siti Rahmawati, 43, a mother of three who was evacuated with her family. "By the time I opened my door, the water was already at my knees. We grabbed the children and climbed to the second floor. We left everything behind — everything."

Another resident, Bambang Suryanto, 56, described the terror of the sudden rush of water. "I have lived here for thirty years, and I have seen floods before, but never like this. This came like a wave, not like the usual slow rising. People did not have time to save their belongings, only their lives."

Rescue officials confirmed that shelters had been established in schools, mosques, and community halls on higher ground, where displaced families received food, blankets, and medical attention. Aid organizations warned of a growing need for clean water and sanitation as the number of evacuees continued to climb.

## Casualties and Damage Still Being Assessed

Authorities cautioned that the full scale of the disaster remained unclear as floodwaters had not yet receded in many areas. Search-and-rescue teams reported difficulty reaching certain neighborhoods where roads were submerged or damaged. Officials urged residents in vulnerable areas to move to designated evacuation points and to avoid attempting to return home until conditions were declared safe.

Preliminary assessments indicated significant damage to homes, vehicles, and local infrastructure. Power was cut to several districts as a precaution, and portions of major roadways were rendered impassable, snarling the region's already notorious traffic.

## A Region Long Vulnerable to Flooding

The disaster underscores a recurring crisis for greater Jakarta, one of the most flood-prone metropolitan regions in the world. Home to more than 30 million people across its sprawling urban area, the capital and its surroundings face seasonal deluges nearly every year during the wet season, which typically runs from November through March.

Several factors compound the region's vulnerability. Jakarta sits on low, swampy ground crossed by more than a dozen rivers, and large parts of the city lie at or below sea level. The problem has been made worse by rapid, often unregulated urban development and by excessive groundwater extraction, which has caused parts of the city to sink at alarming rates — in some areas by several centimeters each year.

Aging water-management infrastructure, much of it dating back decades, has struggled to keep pace with intensifying rainfall and a booming population. Environmental experts have long warned that climate change is producing heavier and more erratic rainfall, placing additional strain on dams, canals, and drainage systems that were not designed for such extremes.

The Indonesian government has for years pursued flood-mitigation projects, including river normalization efforts, reservoir construction, and a massive coastal sea wall initiative. Concerns over Jakarta's flooding and subsidence have been so severe that authorities have moved forward with plans to relocate the national capital to a new site on the island of Borneo.

## Officials Pledge Response and Investigation

Government representatives said emergency resources were being mobilized and pledged a full investigation into the dam's failure, including whether maintenance shortfalls or design limitations contributed to the collapse. Disaster management officials appealed for patience and cooperation from the public as relief operations expanded.

Meteorological agencies warned that additional rainfall was possible in the coming days, raising fears of further flooding and hampering recovery work. Residents were advised to remain vigilant and heed official warnings.

For families like Siti Rahmawati's, the immediate concern is survival and shelter, but the longer-term questions loom large. "We will rebuild, because this is our home," she said, gazing at the water still covering her street. "But how many more times must we lose everything before something changes?"
